description: We are a group of students from Troy High School, Fullerton, and we are very excited to be a part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge in 2026! Our names are Avi Lee, Pratheek Danam, Steven Liang, Ismail Churaev, Ryan Jian, and Daniel Li. We have learned a lot over the course of the entire competition and having the chance working together on this project was a great blessing. Thank you to the NASA Space Apps team for organizing this hackathon!
summary:
The ground in California's San Joaquin Valley is dynamic. Every wet season the ground lifts several centimeters as aquifers fill. Then, every dry season it subsides. However, there are areas of the valley that are consistently subsiding causing problems in canals, levees and wells. When comparing only two points in time from satellite data it can be difficult to distinguish between the dynamic ground and subsidence.

This project uses all 26 passes of NISAR's L-band radar in the first year of operation (November 2025 to October 2026). This allows us to distinguish which pixels are dynamically uplifting and which are subsiding. Each pixel has an associated uncertainty and is simply labelled as uplifting, subsiding, both or insufficient evidence. Our radar has been validated using data from 13 GPS stations which were not seen by the radar during processing. The data agree well with our data to ~1.8cm over every 12 day pair. 41% of the pixels have subsided past their uncertainties by up to 16.3cm.

Our map provides an insight into every measurement. An animation of our data in 3D allows everyone to have a better understanding. There is agreement with GPS and where the numbers come from.
details:
Problem

Land in the San Joaquin Valley in California experiences both expansion and compression as the water table rises during wet periods and falls during pumping. However, there is also a long-term land subsidence throughout certain areas of the valley. Every year the land will expand however it won’t subside. The capacity of the Friant-Kern Canal has reduced up to 60% due to land subsidence causing issues with the wells used by many communities. Current methods of monitoring land subsidence use two points in time from satellite imagery which makes it impossible to identify whether subsidence or expansion is occurring. If the wrong two points are chosen it appears that the land is stable.

Why?

The decrease in water pressure due to pumping means the sediment layers will subside. However, when the water returns, the earth can bounce back. In many areas it will not.

Why NISAR?

NISAR radar has a long wavelength (24cm) meaning it provides more reliable results than short wavelengths. The satellite has a revisit time of 12 days meaning the radar can be compared to give the displacement of the land. We used the first year of NISAR over the valley.

Results

By using all 26 passes of NISAR we were able to fit a sine wave (seasonal changes/expansion) and trends (subsidence) to each cell in the map with their uncertainties. Each cell was assigned one of four categories (Expansion & Subsidence: 22%, Subsidence Only: 6%, Expansion Only: 10%, Not enough evidence: 62%). From the land that NISAR was able to measure reliably, 41% of it had subsided by greater than the uncertainty over 11 months. We compared NISAR radar data to 13 GPS stations (Blind test) and they agree to within ~1.8cm over 12 days.

Breathing Ground

There are 3 sections to the Breathing Ground.

Story

This section has interactive information throughout. There is an interactive cross-section of an aquifer that can be drained and filled. There is a slider to see the radar fringes depending on the ground displacement. There is a graph that can be scrolled through to see 11 months of NISAR and GPS data. There is a game to compare 2 dates with the real GPS station and see how stable the subsiding land appears.

Map

There are 7 different maps (Net Displacement, Any 2 Dates, Time Lapse (Pass by Pass), Radar Fringes, Evidence (4 types), Hidden Subsidence & Patterns). By clicking anywhere on the map you can view all 26 measurements, uncertainty, GPS comparison and source of each number. There are tools to view a profile of the California Aqueduct, draw cross-sections, 3D view, Swipe View, Radar View, Crop Field Polarisation, Groundwater Wells, Walkthrough & Shareable Links.

Dance

The whole year becomes a 3D animation with audio. Each square km in the valley has a dot that expands and contracts depending on how the radar is affected by each pass. Each pass is a beat in the music and if there is no pass there is no sound.

New Features

Hidden subsidence highlights the areas of expansion (When 2 dates have been taken, months apart showing the land expanding but in reality the whole record shows it subsiding). This is the exact area that would trick people using 2 dates. Uncertainty is measured against independent GPS. The map only shows areas of expansion/subsidence if there is statistically significant evidence, all other areas are shown as ‘Not enough evidence’.

Connections

The map connects the data to the land. The profile of the California Aqueduct shows the movement along the canal. The groundwater wells layer shows where the 481 state groundwater monitoring wells are (218 are clearly subsiding). The GPS stations have 10 years history of Sentinel-1 giving context to the 1st year of NISAR.

Polarisation

NISAR has 2 polarisations of data (HH & HV). Almond orchards had the highest HV compared to HH (Median -6.1db), compared to alfalfa (-7.7db) and cotton (-7.9db). This is consistent with the branching structure having more backscatter. We only claim what the crop labels show.

Process

We only downloaded the required section of each NISAR GUNW interferogram from ASF (Rather than 54GB). We applied the ionospheric correction from NISAR to each pair. All data was referenced to GPS station P304. Unreliable pixels were masked out using coherence & connected components. We checked each pair for unwrapping errors (Jumps of approx 12cm). We fit the sine & trend terms simultaneously to each pair of dates for each cell. To compare with GPS we projected the east, north & vertical movements of each station to match the direction the radar was looking. The processing was done in Python (numpy, scipy, xarray, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, earthaccess). The website was made in React, Vite, MapLibre GL & Tailwind CSS (GitHub Pages). The dance was written manually in WebGL. It runs in any browser and on phones.

Who is it for?

California has ground water laws meaning local agencies need to monitor land subsidence caused by pumping. This tool can show them where the subsidence is ongoing and how confident we are. All numbers have sources meaning the evidence can be checked. The story and dance make the science clear to anyone.

Limitations/ Future Use

The NISAR data is still preliminary. As there is less than 1 year of data we cannot fully separate the expansion and subsidence. We cannot estimate how much of the subsidence is permanent or how much groundwater storage has been lost. Towards the eastern edge of the area there is less subsidence shown in the radar (2-3cm less) compared to GPS. When more data is released from NISAR we could apply this technique to separate expansion and subsidence every 12 days in any pumped farm basins NISAR covers, from California to Punjab (India), Mexico City & Tehran.
